Commenter says it's a shame xAI exfiltrated private data, because the model is 'actually good (better than opus 4.8 imo)' and the harness is 'butter smooth with the potential of being the best out there.'

Criticism of the open-sourced code: 182 top-level external dependencies and about 1.3 million lines of Rust, called 'slop'. Another user said it's 'an incredible amount of code for what it offers' and doesn't look intentionally designed.
A user says reverse engineering how Grok Build works had been 'a pain in the ass', and the source release will make that easier.
Recommendation: use pi.dev instead of Grok Build with your xAI subscription 'at this point'.

Forks appeared soon after open-sourcing. Examples: a 'VSCodium-style privacy fork' that strips vendor telemetry and blocks x.ai auto-update, multi-provider CLIs, a Tauri desktop GUI, and a Windows telemetry-disable script.
Users note that Issues and Discussions are disabled on the open-source grok-build GitHub repo.

Users say xAI's claim that uploaded user data was or will be deleted isn't trustworthy without independent destruction certificates. One called the open-sourcing 'smoke and mirrors' until it's proven the bucket is empty.
A user who reviewed the codebase found surprising pieces, such as a self-contained terminal renderer that draws a subset of Mermaid diagram types with Unicode box-drawing.

Quoted from the wire-level analysis: 'It uploads the whole repository — every tracked file's content plus git history — independent of what the agent reads.' The user says pricing is competitive and grok-4.5 is good enough, but they chose not to use xAI for this reason.

Reported in the analysis: the 'Improve the model' toggle makes no difference. With it ON or OFF, the whole repo is uploaded the same way, and files read, including a .env secrets file, are sent verbatim and unredacted.

Workaround: disable repo upload in config with [harness] disable_codebase_upload=true. Another user (by asking the Grok CLI itself, unverified) also set [telemetry] trace_upload=false and [features] telemetry=false in ~/.grok/config.toml.

'Grok Build has had impressive performance in a couple of my projects. And fast. So this revelation has been very disappointing.' The user says the upload behavior should be clearly stated in the ToS, noting that only the enterprise plan offers ZDR.

Workaround: a user runs a CLIProxyAPI fork with xAI OAuth so their Grok subscription works from other clients (Claude Code, Pi, Codex). They're bummed because they really like the Grok Build client: 'The TUI is great in the ways that matter' without being flashy.

Mitigation: a user separates coding tools from LLM providers and sandboxes them with bubblewrap. Access is limited to the project dir with read-only .git, and network goes through a proxy that only allows LLM provider hosts.
Skeptic: the gist reporting the upload behavior appears AI-generated, so they want independent reproduction before fully trusting its findings.
Follow-up testing by the security researcher reportedly showed the Grok Build CLI uploads git repositories to a Google Cloud bucket.
At launch, a commenter said it was only for SuperGrok Heavy ($300/month) subscribers, too expensive to compare against competitors. Another saw Heavy on sale at $99/month for 6 months.

A user already paying $40/month couldn't get past the interactive prompt because it's gated on a higher subscription. They found the TUI 'quite beautiful' and built in Rust (Ratatui). On Windows, the binary ran in Nushell with only a slow first startup, but they couldn't test past login.
Positive: headless mode (-p) for scripts and automations, plus full ACP support for building custom bots and orchestration, similar to OpenAI's approach.
Skeptics say it's 'more expensive, as good or worse at the job'. They prefer open-source OpenCode and Pi agent as more customizable than proprietary options.
